hook: A nurse records a patient's temperature every few hours, and a lab logs a reaction's concentration every few seconds. Nobody hands you a formula. Yet the question is still "how fast is it changing right now?" With a table, a graph or a calculator, you can estimate a derivative from the data you actually have.

ideas: From a table, estimate $f'(a)$ by $\frac{f(b) - f(c)}{b - c}$ with $c < a < b$: the two closest data points on either side of $a$.
At the end of a table, only one side exists: use the closest one-sided quotient.
The symmetric difference quotient $\frac{f(a + h) - f(a - h)}{2h}$ averages the left and right quotients and is usually the most accurate.
A numerical derivative on a graphing calculator gives a decimal estimate of $f'(a)$; report it to three decimal places.
From a graph, read the slope of the tangent line from two points on it.

misconception.wrong: To estimate $P'(4)$ from $P(3) = 20$ and $P(5) = 34$, average the values: $P'(4) \approx 27$.
misconception.right: Averaging values estimates $P(4)$, a value. A derivative is a rate: $P'(4) \approx \frac{34 - 20}{5 - 3} = 7$, in output units per input unit.

summary: With data instead of a formula, estimate $f'(a)$ with a difference quotient from two table inputs on either side of $a$, as close as possible, and give the units. A symmetric quotient is the best simple estimate; a calculator's numerical derivative does the same with a tiny $h$, reported to three decimal places.
